---
title: "Why Transformers"
subtitle: "The sequence-processing problem self-attention changed, and why the architecture spread"
---

*Prerequisites: none beyond ordinary reasoning about sequences and counting
steps; `learn/neural-networks.qmd`'s vocabulary (units, layers, parameters)
is useful background but not assumed.*

This lesson explains **why** the transformer architecture takes the shape
it does and why it became the dominant architecture for large language
models. It does not explain **how** self-attention computes its weights;
that is a separate lesson.

## 1. The problem being solved

Before transformers, **recurrent** networks were among the established
approaches to sequence modeling (a sentence, a time series), with long
short-term memory (LSTM) networks and other gated variants especially
prominent. Convolutional sequence models were another important approach.
[S-21] Recurrence is the clearest case of the sequential dependency the
transformer removed, so it is the one worked through here.

A recurrent network reads the sequence one position at a time, carrying
forward a running summary — a "hidden state" — from each step to the next.
Two consequences follow:

- **relating two distant positions takes many steps.** If position 8 in a
  sequence needs information from position 2, that information has to be
  carried forward through every position in between, one step at a time;
- **the computation is one-step-at-a-time.** The summary at step $t$,
  $h_t$, depends on $h_{t-1}$, so $h_t$ cannot be computed until $h_{t-1}$
  is available.

Computer-science writing summarizes "how many steps does this take, as the
input grows?" with a shorthand called **big-O notation**: $O(n)$ means the
number of steps grows in direct proportion to the input size $n$; $O(1)$
means it stays constant, however large $n$ gets. This lesson uses that
shorthand alongside a plain-language restatement each time.

## 2. Recurrence and its sequential dependency

Consider a toy sequence of $n = 8$ tokens, where correctly resolving what
"it" (at position 8) refers to requires relating it back to an antecedent
at position 2. A recurrent network computes the running summary $h_t$
from the previous summary $h_{t-1}$ and the input at step $t$:

> "Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol
> positions of the input and output sequences... This inherently
> sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples,
> which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths." [S-16]

For the $n=8$ example: relating position 2 to position 8 takes
**6 sequential steps** ($2 \to 3$, $3 \to 4$, and so on to $7 \to 8$). The
longest path in the sequence, from position 1 to position 8, takes
**7 sequential steps**. Processing all eight positions once requires
**8 sequential steps** in total, one per position. These figures are this
course's own concrete instantiation of the general pattern Vaswani et
al.'s Table 1 states for recurrent layers: the number of sequential
operations and the longest path between two positions both grow in direct
proportion to sequence length — $O(n)$. [S-16]
`scripts/check_transformer_path_lengths.py` confirms the toy figures and
the general growth pattern across several sequence lengths.

## 3. What self-attention changed

Self-attention lets a position read directly from other positions in a
single layer, rather than relaying information through the positions in
between. Which positions are permitted depends on the setting. In an
**encoder** (bidirectional self-attention), every position may attend to
every other position. In the **decoder** used by an autoregressive
language model, a position can attend to itself and earlier positions,
but not future positions. During training, this causal masking prevents
each position from using later tokens, preserving the next-token
prediction problem. [S-22]

Either way, for the $n=8$ example, position 8 can attend directly to
position 2, in one step, regardless of the six positions between them.
Table 1 states this generally: a self-attention layer connects any two
permitted positions using a number of sequential operations, and a
longest path, that both stay constant no matter how long the sequence
is — $O(1)$ in both cases, unlike recurrence's $O(n)$. [S-17]

This is a **connectivity** property of one attention layer — what a
position is *able* to read directly. It is not a guarantee that training
actually learns to use that connection correctly for a given task.

## 4. Two consequences

**Parallel computation during training.** Because a recurrent layer's
step $t$ needs step $t-1$'s completed summary (§2), a recurrent network's
positions cannot be computed side by side within one training example. A
self-attention layer has no such dependency between positions within a
layer: given the full input, every position's computation can proceed at
the same time. The paper notes that its dot-product attention "can be
implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code," and that
removing recurrence "allows for significantly more parallelization."
[S-23]

**Shorter computational paths.** The longest path between any two
permitted positions — how many sequential steps information must cross to
connect them — drops from growing with sequence length (recurrence) to
staying constant (self-attention). The paper's stated reason this matters:
"The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the
input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range
dependencies." [S-17] Easier to learn, not automatic — and whether a
transformer or a recurrent network is better on a given task remains
task- and setting-dependent.

## 5. Why transformers became prevalent

No single property or paper caused transformers to become the dominant
architecture for large language models. The explanation has layers.

1. **Architecture.** Reduced sequential dependence and constant path
   length, as above. [S-16] [S-17]
2. **Empirical success of the original design.** The paper reported
   translation results that were superior in quality to the recurrent and
   convolutional models it compared against, while being more
   parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. [S-21]
3. **Pretraining and transfer.** Transformer models pretrained on large
   amounts of unlabeled text became reusable across many downstream tasks:
   BERT reported that its pretrained model "can be fine-tuned with just one
   additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide
   range of tasks." [S-24]
4. **Scaling and in-context behavior.** Later transformer language models
   improved systematically with scale: one study reported that loss
   "scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of
   compute used for training," across a wide range. [S-25] GPT-3, a
   175-billion-parameter autoregressive transformer, was applied "without
   any gradient updates or fine-tuning," with tasks and a few
   demonstrations specified purely in the input text, and showed that
   scaling up "greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance."
   [S-26]

These developments together
help explain why transformers became the dominant architecture for large
language models: prevalence emerged from the combination of architectural
advantages and subsequent empirical success, not from any one of them.
[S-20]

## 6. Cost and limitations

Self-attention is not free. Table 1 also states that its arithmetic cost
per layer grows with the *square* of sequence length — written
$O(n^2 \cdot d)$, where $n$ is sequence length and $d$ is the length of
the vector representing each position. [S-17] In plain language: holding
$d$ fixed, doubling the length of the input roughly quadruples that
component of the arithmetic. This is a real and frequently-cited
limitation once $n$ grows large. Two things this claim is *not*: it is a
statement about how much arithmetic is required, not about how much
computer memory any particular implementation needs to hold while doing
that arithmetic; and it is not a lower bound for every possible
attention-like method (Table 1's "Self-Attention (restricted)" row uses a
fixed-size neighborhood to reduce the cost). The growing-with-the-square
cost has motivated a range of alternatives — attention restricted to
nearby or selected positions, variants with a gentler growth rate, and
different architectures altogether — as an active area of research.
[S-18]

## 7. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>For a recurrent network processing a sequence of length $n$, how
does the longest path between the two most distant positions grow as $n$
grows, and why?</summary>
It grows in direct proportion to $n$ — for the toy $n=8$ example, 7
sequential steps between positions 1 and 8. Information must pass through
every intervening position's running summary, one step at a time, because
each step's computation depends on the previous step finishing first (§2).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Why can a self-attention layer's positions be computed side by
side during training, when a recurrent layer's cannot?</summary>
A recurrent layer's step $t$ depends on step $t-1$'s completed summary,
so steps must run in order. A self-attention layer has no such
dependency between positions within the layer — given the full input,
every position's computation can start at the same time (§4).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>True or false: a one-layer self-attention network is guaranteed
to correctly resolve any long-range dependency in its input.</summary>
False. A constant-length path means a position *can* read any permitted
earlier position in one step; it does not guarantee the network has
learned to use that connection correctly for a given task (§3).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Is standard self-attention's square-in-sequence-length cost a
claim about computer memory, or about arithmetic?</summary>
Arithmetic. It is the number of computational operations per layer, not a
statement about how much memory any specific implementation needs to use
to perform that computation (§6).
</details>
:::

## 8. Continue learning

- **Vaswani et al., *Attention Is All You Need*** (paper; Sections 1 and 4
  are the relevant sections for this lesson, a few pages). Technical
  level. The original source for every growth-rate figure in this lesson,
  including Table 1's full comparison across layer types. Limitation:
  written for a machine-translation encoder-decoder setting, not a modern
  decoder-only language model — the architectural comparison in this
  lesson still holds, but read the paper's own framing with that context
  in mind. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>

- **Devlin et al., *BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers
  for Language Understanding*** (paper; the abstract and introduction are
  enough for §5's point). Technical level. The source for the
  pretraining-and-transfer layer of §5. Limitation: an encoder model, not
  an autoregressive language model. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805>

- **Kaplan et al., *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*** (paper;
  the abstract states the result used in §5). Technical level. Limitation:
  an empirical regularity over the studied range and setup, not a law.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361>

- **Brown et al., *Language Models are Few-Shot Learners*** (paper; the
  abstract states the results used in §5). Technical level. Limitation:
  reports observed task performance from in-context demonstrations; it
  does not explain the mechanism. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165>

- **3Blue1Brown, *Transformers, the tech behind LLMs*** (video; the
  segment starting at 3:03, "inside a transformer," runs a few minutes;
  full video is part of a longer series). Introductory/visual level. Shows
  a transformer block's overall shape visually, as background for the
  architectural claims made throughout this lesson. Limitation: does not
  derive the path-length or complexity arguments in §2–§6 above.
  <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gpt>
